title: Sen. Cornyn Threatens To Block Trump Ambassador Picks Over PEPFAR Funding Cuts
excerpt: The outgoing Texas Republican is leveraging Senate confirmation power to pressure the Trump administration into restoring funding for the global AIDS prevention program that has saved over 26 million lives.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Sen. Cornyn threatens to block Trump ambassador nominees over PEPFAR funding cuts.
  • PEPFAR funding may drop from $6.5 billion to $2.9 billion in FY2026.
  • Bipartisan senators urge safeguarding PEPFAR funding in FY2027 appropriations.
  • 85% of CDC's global presence could vanish within two years under current plans.
https://x.com/remarks/status/2079684245727981915

A Republican Breaks Ranks on Global Health

Sen. John Cornyn, the veteran Texas Republican who once spearheaded rules changes to speed up confirmation of President Trump's nominees, is now threatening to use the very same Senate procedural tools to block them — over the administration's systematic dismantling of the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR.

Cornyn, who sits on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and is serving out his final term after losing a bitter primary to Trump-backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, has signaled he will place holds on pending ambassador nominations until the administration restores funding for the global health program that has been credited with saving more than 26 million lives since its launch by President George W. Bush in 2003, Politico first reported.

The threat marks a striking reversal for a senator who as recently as October 2025 was pushing to confirm ambassador nominees en bloc and blasting Democrats for what he called "naked partisan obstruction" of the confirmation process.

![President Trump. John Cornyn (R-TX) has threatened to place holds on President Trump's ambassador nominees unless the administration reverses course on cuts to PEPFAR, the landmark global AIDS prevention program.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/13/Official_Presidential_Portrait_of_President_Donald_J._Trump_%282025%29_%28cropped%29%282%29.jpg)

The Unraveling of PEPFAR

> **"Raphael Warnock
25
Sen."**

Cornyn's move comes amid a broader bipartisan rebellion against the Trump administration's restructuring of America's premier global health initiative. The State Department announced on May 5, 2026 that long-standing interagency transfers of PEPFAR resources to the CDC in most countries would end by September 30, effectively forcing partner nations to purchase CDC services and expertise at set fees.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has requested that PEPFAR's budget be slashed from roughly $6.5 billion in the current fiscal year to $2.9 billion for FY2026. The Office of Management and Budget under Director Russell Vought had earlier attempted a "pocket rescission" to cancel $4.9 billion earmarked for HIV/AIDS prevention and global health programs.

"No global health program better demonstrates the success of the U.S. global health strategy and the leadership of CDC than PEPFAR."

— Sens. Raphael Warnock and Bill Cassidy, in a bipartisan letter to appropriations leaders

In late June 2026, Senators Warnock and Cassidy led 23 colleagues — including Republican Bill Cassidy of Louisiana — in urging the Senate Appropriations Committee to directly transfer $2 billion allocated for PEPFAR from the State Department to the CDC's budget. The letter warned that the administration's changes would "cost lives and make our country less safe."

CDC's Global Footprint at Risk

Eight former CDC directors, spanning Republican and Democratic administrations, published a joint appeal in STAT News in May 2026 warning that the State Department's approach would rapidly dismantle America's overseas public health capability. Without a managed transition, they wrote, at least 18 CDC global outposts could close before the end of 2026, and up to 85% of CDC's global presence could evaporate within two years.

The former directors — including Robert Redfield, who served under Trump during his first term, and Rochelle Walensky from the Biden era — noted that CDC's overseas offices are not just AIDS infrastructure. They are the same facilities that detect and respond to disease outbreaks like the recent Ebola crisis in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda, and the hantavirus cluster linked to a Dutch cruise ship.

The dismantling follows the official closure of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) on July 1, 2025, which had served as another key implementing partner for PEPFAR alongside the CDC and State Department.

The India Connection

India has been a significant beneficiary of PEPFAR since the program's early years. The country, home to the world's third-largest population of people living with HIV, has received hundreds of millions in PEPFAR support for antiretroviral treatment, prevention, and laboratory infrastructure. Indian pharmaceutical companies have also been central to the program's success, manufacturing the generic antiretroviral drugs that made large-scale treatment affordable across Africa and Asia.

Reports that the State Department has begun conditioning PEPFAR assistance on economic concessions — including favorable access to critical mineral resources, as alleged in Zambia — have raised alarm among Indian-American advocacy groups. Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Brian Schatz, and Chris Coons wrote to Secretary Rubio in April 2026, calling the practice "a disturbing break from the long-held bipartisan support for PEPFAR."

What's Next

Cornyn's threat adds Republican leverage to what has been primarily a Democratic-led pushback on PEPFAR cuts. With the September 30 deadline for ending interagency funding transfers approaching, the FY2027 appropriations process becomes the critical battleground. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee currently has dozens of ambassador nominees awaiting confirmation, giving Cornyn significant leverage.

The outgoing senator has already demonstrated a willingness to break with the administration on other fronts, including withholding his vote on Trump's attorney general nominee Todd Blanche and refusing to campaign for Paxton in a Texas Senate race that Democrats are aggressively targeting.

Whether Cornyn's move pressures the White House to reverse course or merely adds to the growing chorus of bipartisan dissent remains to be seen. But the spectacle of a senior Republican using confirmation holds — a tactic he once condemned — to defend a George W. Bush-era program against a fellow Republican president underscores just how far the intraparty fight over PEPFAR has escalated.
